EXP_BERN: exponential Bernoulli mixture model

Source: vignettes/expbern.Rmd
expbern.Rmd
library(bssd)

Model

The exponential Bernoulli (EXP_BERN) model of Duncan (2026, Section 3.3) assumes constant hazard rates, like BDRIBS, but models whether each subject had the event during the individual follow-up time instead of the number of subjects with the event. For subject \(i\) with the follow-up time \(t_i\), the event indicator \(Y_i\) follows the mixture of two Bernoulli distributions, \[P(Y_i = 1) = w_p \{1 - \exp(-\lambda_p t_i)\} + w_d \{1 - \exp(-r \lambda_p t_i)\},\] where \(w_p = 1 / (k + 1)\) and \(w_d = k / (k + 1)\) are the proportions of subjects on placebo and on the study drug for the randomization ratio \(k:1\), \(\lambda_p\) is the hazard rate on placebo and \(r\) is the rate ratio of the study drug to placebo. The priors are \[\lambda_p \sim \mathrm{Gamma}(\lambda_{HP} PT_{HP} / DF, PT_{HP} / DF), \quad r = \frac{p}{k (1 - p)}, \quad p \sim \mathrm{Beta}(a, b),\] with the shape and rate parameterization of the Gamma distribution, as in BDRIBS (vignette("bdribs1")). Duncan (2026) uses the Beta(0.5, 0.5) prior for \(p\). A signal is declared when \(P(r > \theta_c \mid \mathrm{data}) > P_{\mathrm{cutoff}}\).

The arguments of expbern_post() correspond to the symbols as follows.

Symbol Argument Description
\(Y_i\) y event indicator of each subject (1 if the subject had the event during follow-up)
\(t_i\) t follow-up time of each subject
\(k\) k randomization ratio of study drug to placebo
\(\lambda_{HP}\) lambda_hp event rate in the historical placebo data
\(PT_{HP}\) pt_hp total patient time of the historical placebo data
\(DF\) df discount factor
\((a, b)\) p_prior shape parameters of the Beta prior of \(p\) (default c(0.5, 0.5))
\(\theta_c\) rr0 critical value of \(r\) (default 1)
\(P_{\mathrm{cutoff}}\) cutoff posterior probability threshold (default 0.95)

t, lambda_hp, pt_hp and the optional time t_star for the cumulative incidences must be in the same time unit. Because the likelihood stays positive as \(r \to \infty\), the posterior mean of \(r\) is infinite when the second shape parameter of the Beta prior is 1 or less, as for the default prior; the posterior median is then the summary of \(r\) to use.

Example

The following data are simulated with sim_blinded(): 300 subjects randomized 1:1 with uniform entry over 26 weeks, 52 weeks of planned follow-up, and exponential times to the event with cumulative incidences of 10% on placebo and 20% on the study drug at week 52. At the blinded analysis at week 52, the follow-up times are between 26 and 52 weeks.

set.seed(2026)
rate_of <- function(ip, t) -log(1 - ip) / t
d <- sim_blinded(n = 300, k = 1, accrual = 26, follow_up = 52,
                 analysis_time = 52, dist = "exponential",
                 par_p = rate_of(0.10, 52), par_d = rate_of(0.20, 52))
head(d[, c("id", "follow_up", "event")])
#>   id follow_up event
#> 1  1  44.36873     0
#> 2  2  42.33813     0
#> 3  3  42.56790     0
#> 4  4  42.60844     0
#> 5  5  31.83289     0
#> 6  6  31.65294     0

The prior of \(\lambda_p\) is based on a historical placebo group of 150 subjects followed for 52 weeks with the incidence of 10%, discounted by \(DF = 2\).

fit <- expbern_post(y = d$event, t = d$follow_up, k = 1,
                    lambda_hp = rate_of(0.10, 52), pt_hp = 150 * 52,
                    df = 2, t_star = 52)
fit
#> Model: EXP_BERN 
#> Relative risk: rate ratio r of study drug to placebo
#> P(r > 1 | data) = 0.751
#> Signal (posterior probability > 0.95): no
#> Posterior of r: mean Inf, median 1.626, 95% interval (0.2321, 5.326)
#> Cumulative incidence at t_star = 52: placebo 0.1094, study drug 0.1638, difference 0.05434
summary(fit)
#>      model      prob signal rr_mean rr_median  rr_lower rr_upper ip_placebo
#> 1 EXP_BERN 0.7510482  FALSE     Inf  1.625838 0.2321424 5.326324  0.1094196
#>     ip_drug ip_difference        error
#> 1 0.1637567    0.05433711 5.669898e-11

The posterior probabilities for other critical values of \(r\) are obtained with rr0; details = FALSE skips the quantiles of \(r\):

vapply(c(1, 1.5, 2), function(q) {
  expbern_post(y = d$event, t = d$follow_up, k = 1,
               lambda_hp = rate_of(0.10, 52), pt_hp = 150 * 52, df = 2,
               rr0 = q, details = FALSE)$prob
}, numeric(1))
#> [1] 0.7510482 0.5476504 0.3748275

Numerical integration

expbern_post() integrates the two-dimensional posterior numerically on the coordinates \(\log \lambda_p\) and the prior distribution function of \(p\). A coarse grid locates the region that holds almost all posterior mass; Gauss-Legendre quadrature is used for \(\log \lambda_p\) and Chebyshev interpolation for the second coordinate (see ?expbern_post). With control$check = TRUE, the default, the computation is repeated on a finer grid, the finer result is returned, and the absolute difference in prob is reported as the error estimate (fit$integration$error, here 5.7e-11).

The script inst/validation/validate_convergence.R compares the default grid with a much finer grid for the following data sets. The column Error estimate is the error estimate reported with the default grid.

Comparison with MCMC

The script inst/validation/validate_jags.R compares expbern_post() with MCMC in JAGS for the simulated data sets below. The JAGS model is written directly from the model specification of Duncan (2026, Section 3.3) and shares no code with bssd:

model {
  for (i in 1:N) {
    pp[i] <- 1 - exp(-lambda * t[i])
    pd[i] <- 1 - exp(-r * lambda * t[i])
    y[i] ~ dbern(wp * pp[i] + (1 - wp) * pd[i])
  }
  lambda ~ dgamma(alpha, beta)
  p ~ dbeta(a, b)
  r <- p / (k * (1 - p))
}

The results in this section are read from the output of that script (validate_jags.csv in the folder validation/results of the installed package); JAGS is not run when this article is built.

Data N k Events Placebo (week 52) Study drug (week 52) Analysis (week) Prior incidence (week 52) Prior of p rr0
E1 150 1 15 10% 20% 52 10% Beta(0.5, 0.5) 1.0
E2 300 1 101 30% 30% 78 30% Beta(0.5, 0.5) 1.0
E3 200 2 4 5% 10% 40 5% Beta(1, 1) 1.5

Placebo and Study drug are the incidences used to simulate the data with sim_blinded(), and Prior incidence is the incidence from which lambda_hp is computed; the script gives the other settings. JAGS was run with 4 chains, 5,000 burn-in iterations and 50,000 iterations per chain. The Monte Carlo standard error (SE) of each MCMC estimate uses the effective sample size of the draws (coda::effectiveSize()); for the posterior probabilities, the effective sample sizes are between 21,753 and 59,895. For the median, the table shows the MCMC proportion of draws below the posterior median computed by bssd, which should be 0.5. The incidences are the posterior means of the cumulative incidences at week 52. The column Ratio is the absolute difference divided by the SE.

In all 12 items, the bssd value is within 1.5 standard errors of the MCMC value, and 12 items are within two standard errors. The largest absolute difference in a posterior probability is 0.0051, while the SEs of the MCMC probabilities are between 0.0013 and 0.0034. Differences of this size are expected from the Monte Carlo error of MCMC alone, so the difference between the numerical integration of bssd and MCMC is negligible in practice. The validation script judges an item PASS when the difference is at most four standard errors; 12 of the 12 items are PASS.

References

Duncan, B. (2026). Robust safety monitoring and signal detection using alternatives to the standard Poisson distribution. Journal of Biopharmaceutical Statistics, 36(2), 227-244. https://doi.org/10.1080/10543406.2024.2395532
